cards.title: In $5^3$, which number is the **base**, which is the **exponent**, and what is the value?
cards.body:
The base $5$ is the number being multiplied, the exponent $3$ counts the copies: $5^3 = 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$.

An **exponent** is the small raised number that says how many copies of the **base** to multiply together.

Example: $2^4 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$.

Watch out: $5^3$ is not $5 \times 3 = 15$. The exponent counts multiplications, it does not multiply.

Tip: $b^2$ is read "b squared" and $b^3$ "b cubed"; for larger exponents say "b to the power of $n$".
cards.searchQuery: exponent base meaning power repeated multiplication
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: What is the **product rule** for exponents: $b^m \times b^n = {?}$ (same base $b$)
cards.body:
$b^m \times b^n = b^{m+n}$

Why: Write the copies out. $2^3 \times 2^2 = (2\cdot 2\cdot 2)(2\cdot 2) = 2^5$. Multiplying the two groups just counts all the copies together, so the exponents add.

Example: $10^2 \times 10^4 = 10^6$, which is $100 \times 10{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000$.

Watch out: The bases must match. $2^3 \times 3^2 = 8 \times 9 = 72$, which is not $6^5 = 7776$.
cards.searchQuery: product rule exponents add same base
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: What is the **power rule** for exponents: $(b^m)^n = {?}$
cards.body:
$(b^m)^n = b^{m \times n}$

Why: $(2^4)^2$ means two copies of $2^4$ multiplied together: $2^4 \times 2^4$. By the product rule that is $2^{4+4} = 2^8$. Adding $4$ twice is the same as multiplying $4 \times 2$.

Example: $(10^3)^2 = 10^6$.

Watch out: Do not mix it up with the product rule. $2^4 \times 2^2 = 2^6$, but $(2^4)^2 = 2^8$.
cards.searchQuery: power rule exponents multiply power of a power
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: What does a **negative exponent** mean, and what is $b^0$ for a nonzero $b$?
cards.body:
$b^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{b^n}$ and $b^0 = 1$.

Look at the pattern as the exponent drops by one: $10^3 = 1000$, $10^2 = 100$, $10^1 = 10$, $10^0 = 1$, $10^{-1} = 0.1$, $10^{-2} = 0.01$. Each step down divides by $10$.

Why: The **quotient rule** says dividing powers of the same base subtracts exponents: $b^m / b^n = b^{m-n}$. Take $b^2 / b^2$: anything divided by itself is $1$, and the rule gives $b^0$. Take $b^2 / b^5 = b^{-3}$, which is also $\frac{1}{b^3}$.

Watch out: A negative exponent does not make the number negative. $2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}$, not $-8$.
cards.searchQuery: negative exponent reciprocal zero exponent equals one
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: What does a **fractional exponent** such as $b^{1/n}$ mean (for $b > 0$)?
cards.body:
$b^{1/n}$ is the $n$th root of $b$, so $b^{1/2} = \sqrt{b}$ and $b^{m/n} = \left(\sqrt[n]{b}\right)^m$.

Why: The power rule gives $(b^{1/2})^2 = b^{(1/2) \times 2} = b^1 = b$. So $b^{1/2}$ is a number that squares to $b$: the square root. The same argument makes $b^{1/3}$ the cube root.

Example: $9^{1/2} = 3$ and $27^{1/3} = 3$, because $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$. Also $16^{3/4} = (\sqrt[4]{16})^3 = 2^3 = 8$.

Tip: In $b^{m/n}$, the bottom number $n$ is the root and the top number $m$ is the power.
cards.searchQuery: fractional exponent nth root rational exponent meaning
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.3 Radicals and Rational Exponents

cards.title: Simplify $10^3 \times 10^{-6}$ (as a power of $10$) and $(2^4)^2$ (as a plain number).
cards.body:
$10^{-3}$ and $256$.

Step 1: The bases match, so add the exponents: $10^3 \times 10^{-6} = 10^{3 + (-6)} = 10^{-3}$, which is $0.001$.

Step 2: Multiply the exponents: $(2^4)^2 = 2^{4 \times 2} = 2^8 = 256$.

Check: $2^4 = 16$ and $16^2 = 256$.

Watch out: $3 + (-6)$ is $-3$, not $+3$. Keep the sign of the negative exponent.
cards.searchQuery: simplify 10^3 times 10^-6 exponent rules (2^4)^2
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: Evaluate $4^{1/2}$ and $8^{2/3}$ without a calculator.
cards.body:
$2$ and $4$.

Step 1: $4^{1/2}$ is the square root of $4$, which is $2$.

Step 2: In $8^{2/3}$ the root is the bottom number $3$ and the power is the top number $2$: $8^{2/3} = (\sqrt[3]{8})^2 = 2^2 = 4$.

Check: Doing the power first gives the same answer: $8^2 = 64$ and $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$.

Tip: Take the root first. It keeps the numbers small and easy to square.
cards.searchQuery: evaluate 4^(1/2) 8^(2/3) fractional exponents
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.3 Radicals and Rational Exponents

cards.title: What is **scientific notation**?
cards.body:
A number written as $a \times 10^n$ with $1 \le a < 10$ and $n$ an integer (it may be negative).

The exponent $n$ tells you the size at a glance, and $a$ holds the significant digits.

Example: $4{,}500{,}000 = 4.5 \times 10^6$ and $0.00032 = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}$. Count how many places the decimal point moves: moving it left gives a positive exponent, moving it right a negative one.

Watch out: $45 \times 10^5$ is not scientific notation, because $a$ must be below $10$. The correct form is $4.5 \times 10^6$.
cards.searchQuery: scientific notation definition a times 10^n
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: What is **engineering notation**?
cards.body:
Scientific notation whose exponent is always a multiple of $3$: $a \times 10^n$ with $n = \ldots, -6, -3, 0, 3, 6, \ldots$ and $1 \le a < 1000$.

Why: Multiples of three line up with the SI prefixes (milli, kilo, mega and so on), so the exponent translates straight into a prefix.

Example: $47{,}000 = 47 \times 10^3$, $0.0022 = 2.2 \times 10^{-3}$ and $0.00000033 = 330 \times 10^{-9}$.

Tip: To change $4.7 \times 10^4$ into engineering form, lower the exponent to the next multiple of three and shift the decimal point to match: $47 \times 10^3$.
cards.searchQuery: engineering notation exponent multiple of three
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: Give the symbol and power of ten for the SI prefixes **pico**, **nano**, **micro** and **milli**.
cards.body:
pico p $= 10^{-12}$, nano n $= 10^{-9}$, micro $\mu = 10^{-6}$, milli m $= 10^{-3}$.

An **SI prefix** is a word-part placed before a unit that multiplies it by a fixed power of ten. Milli plus ampere gives milliampere, one thousandth of an ampere.

Example: $1\,\mathrm{ms} = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}$ and $1\,\mathrm{ns} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{s}$, so $1\,\mathrm{ms} = 10^6\,\mathrm{ns}$.

Watch out: Lowercase m is milli and uppercase M is mega. $1\,\mathrm{mW}$ is a thousandth of a watt, $1\,\mathrm{MW}$ is a million watts.
cards.searchQuery: SI prefixes pico nano micro milli powers of ten
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards
BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, table of SI prefixes

cards.title: Give the symbol and power of ten for the SI prefixes **kilo**, **mega**, **giga** and **tera**.
cards.body:
kilo k $= 10^3$, mega M $= 10^6$, giga G $= 10^9$, tera T $= 10^{12}$.

Each prefix is a factor of $1000$ bigger than the one before.

Example: A processor clock of $2.4\,\mathrm{GHz}$ is $2.4 \times 10^9$ cycles per second.

Watch out: Kilo is a lowercase k. Capital K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature.

Watch out: For data, this course uses $1\,\mathrm{kB} = 1000$ bytes and $1\,\mathrm{KiB} = 1024$ bytes. The SI prefix always means a power of ten.
cards.searchQuery: SI prefixes kilo mega giga tera powers of ten
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards
BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, table of SI prefixes

cards.title: Convert $4.7\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ to ohms by swapping the prefix for its power of ten.
cards.body:
$4.7\,\mathrm{k\Omega} = 4.7 \times 10^3\,\Omega = 4700\,\Omega$.

The symbol $\Omega$ stands for the ohm, the unit of electrical resistance (how strongly a part opposes electric current). You will meet it properly later; here it is just a unit with a prefix.

Method: Replace the prefix by its power of ten, then multiply. Kilo is $10^3$, so the decimal point moves three places to the right.

Example: Going back, $2200\,\Omega = 2.2 \times 10^3\,\Omega = 2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$.

Watch out: A prefix that makes the unit bigger makes the number smaller. $4700\,\Omega$ is $4.7$ in kilo-ohms.
cards.searchQuery: convert 4.7 kilohm to ohms prefix power of ten
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: A sensor draws $20\,\mathrm{mA}$. Express this in amperes (A), the unit of electric current. Give the number only.
cards.body:
$0.02\,\mathrm{A}$

Milli means $10^{-3}$, so $20\,\mathrm{mA} = 20 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A} = 0.02\,\mathrm{A}$.

Check: $1000\,\mathrm{mA} = 1\,\mathrm{A}$, so $20\,\mathrm{mA}$ must be a small fraction of an ampere.

Tip: Dividing by $1000$ moves the decimal point three places left: $20.0 \to 0.020$.
cards.searchQuery: 20 mA in amperes milli conversion 0.02
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: Convert $250\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ to milliseconds. Give the number only.
cards.body:
$0.25\,\mathrm{ms}$

Route through seconds: $250\,\mu\mathrm{s} = 250 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s} = 0.25\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Why: One millisecond is $1000$ microseconds, so a microsecond is a smaller unit and you need fewer milliseconds than microseconds.

Watch out: The number gets smaller when you move to the bigger unit. An answer of $250{,}000$ has gone the wrong way.
cards.searchQuery: 250 microseconds to milliseconds conversion 0.25 ms
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: Compute $(4 \times 10^5) \times (5 \times 10^{-8})$ and write the result in scientific notation.
cards.body:
$2 \times 10^{-2}$

Step 1: Multiply the numbers in front: $4 \times 5 = 20$.

Step 2: Add the exponents, since the powers of ten share a base: $5 + (-8) = -3$. So the product is $20 \times 10^{-3}$.

Step 3: $20$ is not below $10$, so fix the form: $20 \times 10^{-3} = 2 \times 10^{-2}$, which is $0.02$.

Check: $400{,}000 \times 0.00000005 = 0.02$.

Tip: Division works the other way: divide the numbers in front and subtract the exponents.
cards.searchQuery: multiply numbers in scientific notation add exponents
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation

cards.title: What are the seven **SI base units**?
cards.body:
Second (s), meter (m), kilogram (kg), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd): time, length, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity (how strong a light source appears).

Every other SI unit is built by combining these seven. For electronics you will use second, meter, kilogram, ampere and kelvin the most.

Watch out: The base unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram. It is the only base unit with a prefix built in.
cards.searchQuery: seven SI base units second meter kilogram ampere kelvin mole candela
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards

cards.title: What is an SI **derived unit**? Give hertz and coulomb as examples.
cards.body:
A derived unit is a combination of base units: $1\,\mathrm{Hz} = 1/\mathrm{s}$ and $1\,\mathrm{C} = 1\,\mathrm{A \cdot s}$.

- **hertz (Hz)**: repeats per second, $1/\mathrm{s}$. A $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ signal repeats once every second.
- **coulomb (C)**: a quantity of electric charge, the charge carried by $1\,\mathrm{A}$ flowing for $1\,\mathrm{s}$.
- **joule (J)**: the unit of energy, $1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{kg \cdot m^2/s^2}$.
- **watt (W)**: the unit of power (energy per second), $1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.

Key idea: Volt and ohm are derived units too; you will build them up when you reach electricity.

Watch out: Units named after people are spelled in lowercase (watt) but their symbols are capitalized (W).
cards.searchQuery: SI derived units hertz coulomb joule watt definition
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards

cards.title: What is a **conversion factor**, and why can you multiply by one without changing the quantity?
cards.body:
A conversion factor is a fraction equal to $1$, such as $\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{m}}{1\,\mathrm{km}}$, so multiplying by it changes the units but not the quantity.

The top and bottom are the same length written in two units, so the fraction is exactly $1$.

Example: $3\,\mathrm{km} \times \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{m}}{1\,\mathrm{km}} = 3000\,\mathrm{m}$. The kilometers cancel like a common factor in a fraction.

Tip: Put the unit you want to get rid of on the bottom of the factor, so it cancels.

Watch out: Flip the fraction and the units do not cancel: $3\,\mathrm{km} \times \frac{1\,\mathrm{km}}{1000\,\mathrm{m}}$ leaves $\mathrm{km^2/m}$, a sign you used the wrong form.
cards.searchQuery: conversion factor fraction equal to one unit conversion cancel
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.3 Unit Conversion

cards.title: A car travels at $72\,\mathrm{km/h}$. What is its speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$? Give the number only.
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Multiply by two conversion factors, one for the distance and one for the time:

$$72\,\frac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{h}} \times \frac{1000\,\mathrm{m}}{1\,\mathrm{km}} \times \frac{1\,\mathrm{h}}{3600\,\mathrm{s}} = \frac{72000}{3600}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} = 20\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$$

Check: Kilometers and hours both cancel, leaving meters per second.

Tip: Dividing a speed in $\mathrm{km/h}$ by $3.6$ gives $\mathrm{m/s}$, because $3600 / 1000 = 3.6$.
cards.searchQuery: convert 72 km/h to m/s conversion factors
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.3 Unit Conversion

cards.title: A student writes $d = v\,t^2$ for distance $d$ in meters, speed $v$ in $\mathrm{m/s}$ and time $t$ in seconds. Using **dimensional analysis** (tracking the units through the equation like algebra), is it consistent?
cards.body:
No: the right side has units $\mathrm{m \cdot s}$, but the left side is in meters.

Dimensional analysis means treating units like algebra symbols and checking that both sides of an equation end up with the same unit.

Step 1: Left side: $d$ is in $\mathrm{m}$.

Step 2: Right side: $v\,t^2 \to \dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \times \mathrm{s}^2 = \mathrm{m \cdot s}$.

Step 3: $\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{m \cdot s}$ differ, so the equation cannot be right.

Fix: $d = v\,t$ works, because $\dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} \times \mathrm{s} = \mathrm{m}$.

Tip: Run this check on any formula you are unsure of.
cards.searchQuery: dimensional analysis check equation units both sides consistent
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.4 Dimensional Analysis

cards.title: Why is it false that an equation passing a units check must be correct?
cards.body:
Dimensional analysis checks only the units, and it cannot see pure numbers, so a wrong constant such as $2$ or $\frac{1}{2}$ still passes.

Example: $d = vt$ and $d = 2vt$ both come out in meters. For a car at $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $5\,\mathrm{s}$, only the first gives the right $50\,\mathrm{m}$; the second says $100\,\mathrm{m}$.

Key idea: A failed units check proves the equation is wrong. A passed check proves only that it is not wrong in its units.

Tip: Use the units check to catch structure errors, such as a missing time or an added quantity with the wrong unit, and test the numbers with a case you can compute by hand.
cards.searchQuery: dimensional analysis limitations wrong constant passes units check
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.4 Dimensional Analysis

cards.title: A current of $0.5\,\mathrm{A}$ flows for $200\,\mathrm{ms}$. Since $1\,\mathrm{C} = 1\,\mathrm{A \cdot s}$, the charge in coulombs is the current in amperes times the time in seconds. How much charge flows? Give the number of coulombs only.
cards.body:
$0.1\,\mathrm{C}$

Step 1: Convert the time to seconds first: $200\,\mathrm{ms} = 200 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s} = 0.2\,\mathrm{s}$.

Step 2: Multiply: $0.5\,\mathrm{A} \times 0.2\,\mathrm{s} = 0.1\,\mathrm{A \cdot s} = 0.1\,\mathrm{C}$.

Watch out: Multiplying $0.5 \times 200 = 100$ mixes amperes with milliseconds. That $100$ is in $\mathrm{A \cdot ms}$, and $100\,\mathrm{A \cdot ms} = 0.1\,\mathrm{C}$, so it is not $100\,\mathrm{C}$. The answer would be $1000$ times too large.

Tip: Before you multiply, write every quantity in base units (A, s, m, kg).
cards.searchQuery: charge coulomb ampere times seconds milliseconds unit error
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.3 Unit Conversion
OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.4 Dimensional Analysis

cards.title: What does $\log_b(x) = y$ mean?
cards.body:
$\log_b(x) = y$ means $b^y = x$: the logarithm is the exponent you must raise $b$ to in order to get $x$.

Example: $\log_2(8) = 3$ because $2^3 = 8$. Likewise $\log_{10}(1000) = 3$, and $\log_{10}(0.01) = -2$ because $10^{-2} = 0.01$.

Key idea: A logarithm counts how many times you multiply by the base.

Watch out: The input $x$ must be positive. No power of a positive base gives zero or a negative number, so $\log_b(0)$ and $\log_b(-5)$ do not exist.
cards.searchQuery: logarithm definition exponent to get x log base b
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.3 Logarithmic Functions

cards.title: Name the **common logarithm**, the **natural logarithm** and the **binary logarithm**: which base does each use and how is each written?
cards.body:
Common: $\log_{10}$, base $10$. Natural: $\ln$, base $e \approx 2.718$. Binary: $\log_2$, base $2$.

The number $e$ is introduced later in this module. For now, treat $\ln$ as a button on the calculator.

Why it matters: Base $10$ fits powers of ten and decibels. Base $2$ fits bits and halving. Base $e$ fits natural growth and decay.

Watch out: A bare "log" is ambiguous. Calculators usually mean $\log_{10}$, computer science often means $\log_2$, and in Python `math.log(x)` is the natural logarithm. Write the base.
cards.searchQuery: common natural binary logarithm log10 ln log2 base
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.3 Logarithmic Functions

cards.title: Why do exponentials and logarithms undo each other? State $\log_b(b^x)$ and $b^{\log_b(x)}$.
cards.body:
They are **inverse functions**: $\log_b(b^x) = x$ and $b^{\log_b(x)} = x$ (for $x > 0$ in the second).

An inverse function is a rule that undoes another rule, like subtracting $5$ undoes adding $5$.

Why: By definition, $\log_b(x)$ is the exponent that turns $b$ into $x$. Raising $b$ to that exponent gives $x$ back. Going the other way, raising $b$ to $x$ and then asking "what exponent?" returns $x$.

Example: $\log_{10}(10^5) = 5$ and $2^{\log_2(7)} = 7$.

Tip: To solve $2^n = 1000$, take $\log_2$ of both sides: $n = \log_2(1000) \approx 9.97$.
cards.searchQuery: logarithm inverse of exponential log_b(b^x) = x
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.3 Logarithmic Functions

cards.title: What is the **product rule** for logarithms: $\log_b(xy) = {?}$ (for $x, y > 0$)
cards.body:
$\log_b(xy) = \log_b(x) + \log_b(y)$

Why: Logarithms are exponents, and exponents add when you multiply powers of the same base: $b^m \times b^n = b^{m+n}$.

Example: $\log_{10}(100 \times 1000) = \log_{10}(10^5) = 5$, and $2 + 3 = 5$.

Key idea: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition. The **quotient rule** is the mirror image: $\log_b(x/y) = \log_b(x) - \log_b(y)$.

Watch out: There is no simple rule for $\log_b(x + y)$. $\log_{10}(10 + 10) = \log_{10}(20) \approx 1.30$, which is not $1 + 1$.
cards.searchQuery: logarithm product rule log of product equals sum of logs
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.5 Logarithmic Properties

cards.title: Evaluate $\log_2(1024)$ without a calculator. Give the number only.
cards.body:
$10$

Ask: what power of $2$ gives $1024$? Double repeatedly: $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024$. That is $10$ doublings, so $2^{10} = 1024$.

Why it matters: This is the same fact as "$10$ bits give $1024$ distinct values". The binary logarithm of the number of values is the number of bits.

Tip: Memorize $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$. It lets you estimate many logs quickly.
cards.searchQuery: log2 1024 equals 10 binary logarithm powers of two
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.3 Logarithmic Functions

cards.title: Given $\log_{10}(2) \approx 0.301$, estimate how many decimal digits $2^{64}$ has (the number of values of a 64-bit unsigned integer).
cards.body:
About $20$ digits: $2^{64} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{19}$.

The **power rule** for logarithms: $\log_b(x^k) = k \log_b(x)$. It follows from the exponent power rule.

Step 1: $\log_{10}(2^{64}) = 64 \times \log_{10}(2) \approx 64 \times 0.301 = 19.26$.

Step 2: So $2^{64} \approx 10^{19.26} = 10^{0.26} \times 10^{19}$, and $10^{0.26} \approx 1.8$.

Step 3: Every number from $10^{19}$ up to just below $10^{20}$ has $20$ digits ($10^{19}$ is a $1$ followed by $19$ zeros). So the count is $19 + 1 = 20$.

Check: The exact value is $18{,}446{,}744{,}073{,}709{,}551{,}616$, which has $20$ digits.
cards.searchQuery: digits of 2^64 logarithm power rule log10 2 0.301
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.5 Logarithmic Properties

cards.title: What is the **change of base** formula for $\log_b(x)$, using logarithms in a new base $c$?
cards.body:
$\log_b(x) = \dfrac{\log_c(x)}{\log_c(b)}$

Why: Let $y = \log_b(x)$, so $b^y = x$. Take $\log_c$ of both sides and use the power rule: $y \log_c(b) = \log_c(x)$. Divide by $\log_c(b)$.

Example: A calculator with only $\log_{10}$ can find $\log_2(1000) = \dfrac{\log_{10}(1000)}{\log_{10}(2)} = \dfrac{3}{0.301} \approx 9.97$.

Watch out: This is a ratio of logs, not the log of a ratio. $\frac{\log_c(x)}{\log_c(b)}$ is not $\log_c(x/b)$.

Tip: Any base $c$ works for the new logs, so use whichever your calculator has, usually $10$ or $e$.
cards.searchQuery: change of base formula logarithm log_b x = log x / log b
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.5 Logarithmic Properties

cards.title: A list has $1000$ candidates. Each test splits the remaining candidates in half (rounding up when the count is odd) and keeps the larger half. At most how many tests leave a single candidate?
cards.body:
$10$ tests, which is $\lceil \log_2(1000) \rceil = 10$.

Halve repeatedly, rounding up: $1000 \to 500 \to 250 \to 125 \to 63 \to 32 \to 16 \to 8 \to 4 \to 2 \to 1$. Counting the arrows gives $10$.

Why: Each test divides the count by $2$, so after $n$ tests about $1000 / 2^n$ remain. We need $2^n \ge 1000$. Since $2^9 = 512 < 1000 \le 1024 = 2^{10}$, $n = 10$.

Check: The change of base formula gives $\log_2(1000) \approx 9.97$, and rounding up gives $10$.

Key idea: This is also how many bits you need to number $1000$ items: $\lceil \log_2(1000) \rceil = 10$.
cards.searchQuery: halvings to reach one ceiling log2 1000 equals 10
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.3 Logarithmic Functions
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.5 Logarithmic Properties

cards.title: What is a **decibel** (dB)? Give the formula that turns a **power ratio** $P_2/P_1$ into decibels.
cards.body:
$L = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right)$ dB, where $P_2/P_1$ is the power ratio.

A **ratio** compares two quantities by dividing one by the other. A **power ratio** compares two powers, measured in watts. The decibel expresses that ratio on a log scale.

Example: Ratio $1$ is $0$ dB, ratio $10$ is $10$ dB, ratio $1000$ is $30$ dB, and ratio $0.1$ is $-10$ dB.

Watch out: A decibel is a ratio, not a unit of anything physical on its own. Negative dB means a loss (output weaker than input), $0$ dB means no change.

Why "deci": A bel is $\log_{10}$ of the ratio, and a decibel is one tenth of a bel.
cards.searchQuery: decibel formula 10 log10 power ratio definition
refs: OpenStax College Physics 2e, §17.3 Sound Intensity and Sound Level
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.3 Logarithmic Functions

cards.title: What is the decibel formula for an **amplitude ratio** $A_2/A_1$ (amplitude: the strength of a signal, for example its voltage)?
cards.body:
$L = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{A_2}{A_1}\right)$ dB

Why: For the same circuit, power goes with the square of the amplitude: $P \propto A^2$. So $10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_2^2}{A_1^2}\right) = 10 \times 2\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)$, by the power rule for logs.

Example: An amplitude ratio of $10$ is $+20$ dB. The power ratio is $10^2 = 100$ and $10\log_{10}(100) = 20$, so the two formulas agree.

Watch out: Using $10$ instead of $20$ for amplitudes gives half the right answer.

refs: OpenStax College Physics 2e, §17.3 Sound Intensity and Sound Level

cards.title: Roughly what power ratio is $+3$ dB, and what amplitude ratio is $+6$ dB?
cards.body:
$+3$ dB is about twice the power, and $+6$ dB is about twice the amplitude.

Why: $10\log_{10}(2) \approx 3.01$ and $20\log_{10}(2) \approx 6.02$.

Example: $-3$ dB halves the power. $+6$ dB is two $+3$ dB steps, so power is $\times 4$, which is the same as amplitude $\times 2$ (power goes with amplitude squared).

Tip: Decibels add where ratios multiply. $+3$ dB then $+10$ dB means power $\times 2 \times 10 = \times 20$, which is about $+13$ dB.
cards.searchQuery: 3 dB double power 6 dB double amplitude rule of thumb
refs: OpenStax College Physics 2e, §17.3 Sound Intensity and Sound Level

cards.title: Why do engineers use decibels to describe quantities such as **dynamic range**?
cards.body:
A log scale squeezes huge ratios into small numbers, and when gains multiply, their decibel values simply add.

**Dynamic range** is the ratio between the largest and the smallest value a system can handle, often quoted in dB.

Example: An unsigned $16$-bit integer runs from $0$ to $65{,}535$, and its smallest nonzero step is $1$. The ratio $65{,}535$ is $20\log_{10}(65{,}535) \approx 96$ dB. Writing "$96$ dB" is far easier than "a ratio of $65{,}535$".

Key idea: A chain of an amplifier giving $+20$ dB and a filter giving $-6$ dB gives $+14$ dB in total. No multiplication is needed.

cards.title: A timer should last $250\,\mathrm{ms}$ but measures $262\,\mathrm{ms}$. What is the **percent error**, to one decimal place? Give the percent value only.
cards.body:
$4.8\%$

Percent error compares the size of the mistake to the true value: $\dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100\%$.

Step 1: Size of the mistake: $|262 - 250| = 12$.

Step 2: Divide by the true value: $12 / 250 = 0.048$.

Step 3: Multiply by $100\%$ to get $4.8\%$.

Watch out: Divide by the true (reference) value. Dividing by the measured value gives $12/262 \approx 4.6\%$, which is wrong.

Tip: **Percent change** has the same shape: $\frac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100\%$, where a negative result is a decrease.
cards.searchQuery: percent error formula measured true value 262 250
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.3 Unit Conversion

cards.title: An amplifier raises a signal's power from $2\,\mathrm{mW}$ to $200\,\mathrm{mW}$. By how many decibels?
cards.body:
$+20$ dB

Step 1: Find the power ratio: $200\,\mathrm{mW} / 2\,\mathrm{mW} = 100$. The units cancel.

Step 2: Apply the power formula: $10\log_{10}(100) = 10 \times 2 = 20$ dB.

Check: $\times 100$ is $\times 10 \times 10$, and each $\times 10$ is $10$ dB, so $10 + 10 = 20$.

Watch out: Use the ratio, not the difference ($200 - 2 = 198$). Also, these are powers, so the factor is $10$. Using $20$ would give $40$ dB.

cards.title: What is **exponential growth**, and what is its **doubling time**?
cards.body:
A quantity that is multiplied by the same factor in every equal time step; the doubling time $T$ is how long one doubling takes, so $N = N_0 \cdot 2^{t/T}$.

Here $N_0$ is the starting value and $N$ the value after time $t$.

Example: A count starts at $3$ and doubles every hour. It goes $3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96$, so after $5$ hours it is $3 \times 2^5 = 96$.

Watch out: After $n$ doublings the value is $N_0 \times 2^n$, not $N_0 \times 2n$.

Key idea: Exponential growth looks slow at first, then explodes.
cards.searchQuery: exponential growth definition doubling time formula N0 2^(t/T)
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.7 Exponential and Logarithmic Models

cards.title: What is **Euler's number** $e$, and roughly how big is it?
cards.body:
$e \approx 2.71828$, the base of the natural logarithm $\ln$ and of the growth and decay curve $e^t$.

Where it comes from: Compute $(1 + 1/n)^n$ for larger and larger $n$. For $n = 1$ you get $2$, for $n = 2$ you get $2.25$, for $n = 10$ about $2.594$, and for $n = 1000$ about $2.717$. The values settle toward $e$.

Why it matters: Curves built on $e$ describe natural processes, such as a capacitor discharging, with the neat property that the curve's steepness at any point is proportional to its height.

Key idea: $\ln(x)$ means $\log_e(x)$, so $\ln(e) = 1$.

Tip: Remember $e^1 \approx 2.7$ and $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$.
cards.searchQuery: Euler's number e 2.71828 natural logarithm base definition
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.7 Exponential and Logarithmic Models

cards.title: In **exponential decay** $N = N_0\,e^{-t/\tau}$, what does the **time constant** $\tau$ mean, and how much of $N_0$ is left at $t = \tau$?
cards.body:
$\tau$ is the time for the quantity to fall to $1/e \approx 37\%$ of its starting value, a drop of about $63\%$.

Exponential decay means the quantity shrinks by the same factor in every equal time step. The curve starts steep and flattens out.

Example: Fraction left after $1\tau$, $2\tau$, $3\tau$, $5\tau$: $e^{-1} \approx 0.368$, $e^{-2} \approx 0.135$, $e^{-3} \approx 0.050$, $e^{-5} \approx 0.007$. After about $5\tau$ the quantity is nearly gone.

Watch out: The curve never reaches exactly zero. Also $\tau$ is not the half-time: the quantity halves after $\tau \ln 2 \approx 0.69\,\tau$.

Why it matters: The charge or voltage in a resistor-capacitor (RC) circuit decays with this shape; you will see this later.

refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.7 Exponential and Logarithmic Models

cards.title: From a table of equally spaced inputs, how can you tell **linear**, **quadratic** and **exponential** growth apart?
cards.body:
Linear: equal differences between neighboring outputs. Quadratic: the differences themselves change by a constant amount. Exponential: equal ratios between neighboring outputs.

Example, for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$:

- Linear $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$: differences $2, 2, 2, 2$.
- Quadratic $0, 1, 4, 9, 16$: differences $1, 3, 5, 7$, which grow by $2$ each time.
- Exponential $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$: ratios $2, 2, 2, 2$.

Watch out: Exponential growth beats quadratic growth eventually, even if it starts lower. At $x = 3$, $x^2 = 9$ beats $2^x = 8$, but from $x = 5$ onward $2^x$ is larger ($32$ against $25$).

Tip: Check differences first, then ratios.
cards.searchQuery: linear quadratic exponential growth table differences ratios
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.7 Exponential and Logarithmic Models

cards.title: Make a **Fermi estimate** (a quick estimate from rough guesses) of how many bytes of plain text are in a $300$-page novel. Say which two powers of ten it lies between.
cards.body:
About $5 \times 10^5$ bytes, which lies between $10^5$ and $10^6$ (roughly $500\,\mathrm{kB}$).

Guess each piece to one digit: $300$ pages $\times$ $300$ words per page $\approx 90{,}000$ words. A word plus its space is about $6$ characters, and one ASCII character is one byte. So $90{,}000 \times 6 = 540{,}000 \approx 5 \times 10^5$ bytes.

The **order of magnitude** of a number is its power of ten. Two values within one order of magnitude differ by less than a factor of $10$.

Why it matters: A Fermi estimate tells you whether an answer is plausible before you build anything. A text file of this book should not be $5\,\mathrm{GB}$.

Tip: Individual guesses may be off, but errors above and below tend to cancel.
cards.searchQuery: Fermi estimate order of magnitude bytes in a novel
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.5 Estimates and Fermi Calculations

cards.title: Start at $1$ and double at every step. How many doublings until the value first exceeds one million ($10^6$)? Give the number only.
cards.body:
$20$

After $n$ doublings the value is $2^n$. We need $2^n > 10^6$.

Step 1: $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$, so $2^{20} \approx (10^3)^2 = 10^6$.

Step 2: Check exactly: $2^{19} = 524{,}288 < 10^6$ and $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576 > 10^6$. So $20$ is the first step that exceeds one million.

Check: $\log_2(10^6) = 6 \times 3.32 \approx 19.93$, and the next whole number is $20$.

cards.title: What is a **function** $f$, and what does $f(3)$ mean?
cards.body:
A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input; $f(3)$ is the output when the input is $3$.

Example: If $f(x) = 2x + 1$, then $f(3) = 2 \times 3 + 1 = 7$.

Why it matters: Engineers describe how one quantity depends on another, such as temperature as a function of time. A graph plots each input against its output.

Watch out: $f(3)$ does not mean $f \times 3$. The parentheses hold the input.

Tip: A graph is a function of $x$ if no vertical line crosses it more than once, because each input has only one output.

refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §3.1 Functions and Function Notation

cards.title: What is the **slope** of the straight line through the points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$?
cards.body:
$\text{slope} = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$, the rise over the run.

The "rise" is the change in the vertical value and the "run" is the change in the horizontal value.

Example: Through $(1, 2)$ and $(5, 10)$ the slope is $\dfrac{10 - 2}{5 - 1} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$.

Key idea: Slope has units: the unit of $y$ per unit of $x$. If $y$ is meters and $x$ is seconds, slope is in $\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: Subtract in the same order on top and bottom. Mixing the order flips the sign.

refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §4.1 Linear Functions

cards.title: In the straight-line equation $y = mx + b$, what do $m$ and $b$ mean on a graph?
cards.body:
$m$ is the slope, the **rate of change** of $y$ per unit of $x$; $b$ is the **intercept**, the value of $y$ where the line crosses the vertical axis (at $x = 0$).

An **axis** is a number line along an edge of the graph. The horizontal axis usually shows the input and the vertical axis the output, each labeled with units.

Example: A heater warms a room as $T = 22 + 3t$ in degrees Celsius with $t$ in minutes. The intercept $22\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is the starting temperature and the slope $3\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ per minute is the rate of change.

Watch out: The intercept $b$ is the value at $x = 0$, not where the line meets the horizontal axis.

refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §4.1 Linear Functions

cards.title: A temperature log reads $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $0\,\mathrm{s}$, $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $10\,\mathrm{s}$, $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $20\,\mathrm{s}$, $55\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $30\,\mathrm{s}$ and $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $40\,\mathrm{s}$. Join the points with straight lines. Where is the graph increasing, decreasing and at its peak, and what is the rate of change in the first $20\,\mathrm{s}$?
cards.body:
Increasing from $0$ to $20\,\mathrm{s}$ at $1.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C/s}$, peak at $20\,\mathrm{s}$ ($60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), decreasing afterwards at $-0.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C/s}$.

A graph is increasing where it rises as you move right (positive slope) and decreasing where it falls (negative slope). The peak is the highest point, where it switches from rising to falling.

Step 1: Rise: $\dfrac{60 - 30}{20 - 0} = 1.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C/s}$.

Step 2: Fall: $\dfrac{50 - 60}{40 - 20} = -0.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C/s}$ (the same as $\frac{55 - 60}{10}$).

Watch out: The sign of the slope gives the direction, and the units tell you what it measures: degrees per second.
cards.searchQuery: graph increasing decreasing peak slope rate of change temperature
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §3.3 Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §4.1 Linear Functions

cards.title: On a **log scale** axis, what does each major gridline represent, and what do equal distances mean?
cards.body:
Each major gridline is ten times the previous one, and equal distances mean equal ratios, not equal differences.

Example: Gridlines labeled $1, 10, 100, 1000, 10{,}000$ are evenly spaced. The step from $10$ to $100$ looks as long as the step from $1000$ to $10{,}000$, although the second is $9000$ units and the first is $90$.

Why: The position along the axis is proportional to $\log_{10}$ of the value.

Watch out: Zero and negative numbers cannot appear on a log axis, because their logarithm does not exist.

Tip: Between two gridlines the labels $2, 3, \ldots, 9$ get closer and closer together. Reading values there is not linear.
cards.searchQuery: log scale axis gridlines factor of ten equal ratios
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.8 Fitting Exponential Models to Data

cards.title: Why is it false that on a log axis the point halfway (in distance) between $10^2$ and $10^4$ is the average, $5050$?
cards.body:
Equal distance means equal ratio, so the halfway point is $10^3 = 1000$, not the average $5050$.

From $100$ to $1000$ the value is multiplied by $10$, and from $1000$ to $10{,}000$ it is multiplied by $10$ again. Both steps take the same distance on the axis, so $1000$ sits in the middle.

Key idea: On an ordinary axis, equal distances are equal differences. On a log axis they are equal factors.

Watch out: Reading a log axis as if it were linear is a common cause of wrong answers. The point $5050$ would sit much closer to the $10^4$ end.
cards.searchQuery: log axis midpoint halfway equal ratio not average misconception
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.8 Fitting Exponential Models to Data

cards.title: Why do exponential data plot as a straight line on a **semi-log plot** (a log axis for $y$, an ordinary axis for $x$)?
cards.body:
Because $y = y_0\,b^x$ gives $\log_{10}(y) = \log_{10}(y_0) + x\,\log_{10}(b)$, a straight line in $x$ with slope $\log_{10}(b)$.

On a semi-log plot only one axis is logarithmic. On a **log-log plot** both are, and power laws $y = k x^p$ become straight lines there.

Example: Doubling data $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$ has $\log_{10}$ values $0, 0.30, 0.60, 0.90, 1.20$: equal steps, so a straight line.

Tip: A steeper line means a bigger growth factor. A line that curves upward on a semi-log plot is growing faster than exponentially.

Why it matters: A straight line on semi-log paper is the quickest check that data are exponential.
cards.searchQuery: semi-log plot exponential straight line log-log plot power law
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.8 Fitting Exponential Models to Data

cards.title: On a semi-log plot (log axis for $y$), a straight line passes through $(t, y) = (0\,\mathrm{s}, 10)$ and $(2\,\mathrm{s}, 1000)$. What is $y$ at $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$?
cards.body:
$y = 10{,}000$, because $y$ is multiplied by $10$ every second.

A straight line on a semi-log plot means $y$ is multiplied by the same factor in every equal time step.

Step 1: From $t = 0$ to $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, $y$ grows from $10$ to $1000$, a factor of $100$.

Step 2: Two equal steps multiply to $100$, so each one-second step is $\times 10$, because $10 \times 10 = 100$.

Step 3: At $3\,\mathrm{s}$: $1000 \times 10 = 10{,}000$.

Check: $\log_{10}(y)$ goes $1 \to 3$ in $2\,\mathrm{s}$, a slope of $1$ per second, so at $3\,\mathrm{s}$ it is $4$ and $y = 10^4$.
cards.searchQuery: semi-log plot straight line read value factor per second
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.8 Fitting Exponential Models to Data
